newsitem.title: USA: U.S. cautiously welcomes Pope's plans to visit Cuba.
newsitem.headline: U.S. cautiously welcomes Pope's plans to visit Cuba.

text.p: The United States on Tuesday cautiously welcomed an announcement that Pope John Paul planned to visit Cuba, saying it would give him a chance to promote human rights on the communist-ruled island.
State Department spokesman Glyn Davies denied that Washington saw the proposed visit as a setback to its policy of trying to isolate Cuba and its president Fidel Castro.
The Pope accepted Castro's invitation to go to Cuba next year during a historic first meeting at the Vatican on Tuesday between the veteran revolutionary and the Catholic leader.
"I don't think we view this as a setback, it's an opportunity," Davies told reporters.

"The Catholic Church has a long history of promoting democracy and protecting human rights. The Pope undoubtedly can play a constructive role in promoting democratic change, and in protecting human rights in Cuba," he said.
"Our hope is if the visit takes place that it will serve to further the cause of freedom for the Cuban people, which is the cause that we've championed for over three decades now."
Driven by what critics said were electoral pressures in the United States, the Clinton administration has steadily tightened sanctions on Cuba.
Last July, Clinton signed into law the Helms-Burton Act, which penalises foreign companies that make use of property in Cuba confiscated from U.S. citizens.
In Brazil, visiting U.S. black leader Rev. Jesse Jackson also welcomed the meeting between Castro and the Pontiff, saying dialogue was the only way to bring about change in Cuba's communist regime.
Jackson, who is attending a "Black Conciousness Week" in Brazil, said he hoped the Pope had won assurances from Castro of greater security for the church in the Caribbean island.
